cards.title: Audit Flash and JavaScript bloat as page-experience obstacles
cards.summary: Treat obsolete Flash embeds and unused or glitchy JavaScript as indexing and speed barriers to clean up on an ecommerce storefront.
cards.use_when: Running a technical SEO audit on your storefront's page experience before paid traffic or a redesign push.
steps: Inventory any remaining Flash elements. The source states web crawlers cannot index Flash files and outdated elements reduce visitor interest, so Flash should be limited rather than occupying whole areas of the page.

Note the source's qualification: limited Flash use can actually help ranking, but heavy Flash slows load speed — the same page-speed struggle you find in the page-speed report. Prefer building product visuals in HTML/CSS where possible.
Check the unused-JavaScript section of your page-speed report. Unused scripts occupy space, slow the site, and show in the red zone, which the source says impacts rankings.

Have a developer clean up dead scripts and JavaScript glitches from the back end. The source frames failure to clean code as something Google reads as a poor impression and that blocks the indexing you want.
Recheck page speed for both desktop and mobile, since Google reports the two separately.
Verify current tool interface locations (page-speed report sections, CMS code access) before relying on any specific menu path.
caveats: The source's Flash advice is largely legacy guidance; Flash is dead technology, so treat this as an illustration of the broader rule that unindexable, heavy embeds hurt stores.
The relationship between page speed and rankings is stated loosely; no numeric speed threshold is given.

cards.title: Confirm your store already has an auto-generated XML sitemap instead of building one
cards.summary: Modern CMS platforms auto-generate XML sitemaps, so verify and submit the existing one rather than generating sitemaps manually.
cards.use_when: Setting up technical SEO for a new store on Shopify, WordPress, or another CMS, especially with hundreds or thousands of product pages.
steps: Check the CMS for a built-in sitemap before reaching for a generator. The source notes WordPress (e.g. RankMath plugin) and Shopify expose sitemap creation as a one-click toggle in the backend, and a site over 500 pages certainly needs one.
Toggle the sitemap setting on and confirm its status. In the source's WordPress example the RankMath sitemap switch was already on.

Verify live visibility by visiting sitemap.xml. The source demonstrates that a WordPress site redirected to sitemap_index.xml instead, listing posts, pages and attachments — expect CMS-specific sitemap URLs.
If a store truly has no sitemap, a free generator such as sitemap-generator.com can produce an HTML or XML file; XML is the format to prefer for search engines.
Submit the sitemap in Google Search Console and reference it in robots.txt so crawlers can find it.
For a store with thousands of SKUs, discuss with your CMS/plugin whether product, collection, image and video sitemaps are generated automatically.
caveats: Sitemap generator tools and CMS sitemap URLs change; verify the current interface before acting.
No fixed page-count rule is supported beyond the source's remark that 500+ pages requires a sitemap.

cards.title: Match sitemap type to audience: XML for crawlers, HTML for shoppers
cards.summary: XML sitemaps feed search bots while HTML sitemaps help human navigation, and each carries a different SEO role.
cards.use_when: Deciding which sitemap to expose when structuring store navigation, a large category tree, or orphaned product pages.
steps: For crawlers, use an XML sitemap. The source states search bots crawl using XML sitemaps and that these are not visible to users. Each URL entry can carry last-modified, modification details and priority — in the demonstration the homepage carried priority 1.0 and other pages lower values like 0.88.

For shoppers, consider an HTML sitemap: a visible list of links guiding visitors to available content. The source says it aids navigation and supplies helpful internal links but has limited SEO value on its own.

Expect different sitemap flavours depending on content type: video sitemaps for /videos, image sitemaps for JPG/PNG/SVG assets, news sitemaps for /article or /news, and product/collection paths on ecommerce sites. WordPress sites surface posts and pages instead.
Once generated, update robots.txt with the sitemap URL and submit via Search Console so crawlers find a store's product and category URLs faster.
If you ever need a text or RSS version, the source notes you can convert between formats, but XML is the most commonly used.
caveats: The source's priority values are illustrative output from a generator, not a prescribed ranking formula.
HTML sitemaps are noted as having limited direct SEO value, so do not treat them as a substitute for clean internal linking.

cards.title: Use Ahrefs keyword difficulty filters to find rankable store keywords
cards.summary: Filter keyword lists by volume and difficulty (KD 0–40) to find terms a new or small store can realistically rank for.
cards.use_when: Choosing which product, category or content keywords to target for a new or low-authority ecommerce store.
steps: Open the keyword research tool's keyword explorer (source uses Ahrefs), enter a seed term and set location to your actual market. The source stresses: if you don't serve Miami, do not target 'Miami SEO agency' style terms.
Read the difficulty band. In the source's example 'SEO' had 247K volume but 'super hard' KD, meaning it is not easy to rank because it is a very general term.
Apply a KD filter of 0–40 for a first phase to surface realistically targetable terms, then scan results for terms you can actually serve.
Exclude terms containing agency names or locations you don't operate in; keep general or service-relevant terms.

Check intent labels: informational, navigational, transactional or commercial. The source shows 'best SEO software' reads as commercial/informational because people want to buy, while 'what is SEO' is informational. Pick keywords whose intent matches your page type.

Inspect the ranking competitors before committing. A term dominated by high-authority sites (domain authority 90+ in the example) is a poor early target — the source warns a very competitive keyword may not appear in the top 100 pages at all.
caveats: Ahrefs KD bands, volumes and filters are tool-specific and change; verify the current interface.
The source's numbers are a demonstration of one keyword, not a benchmark for any other term.

cards.title: Mine question keywords and filter by KD when planning store content
cards.summary: Question-based informational keywords reveal what shoppers ask, and filtering to low difficulty helps new stores rank for them.
cards.use_when: Planning blog, guide or FAQ content that supports an ecommerce store's SEO and attracts early-stage shoppers.
steps: In the keyword tool, open the 'questions people ask' section for your seed term (e.g. SEO shows 'what is SEO', 'what is SEO audit', 'is SEO dead', 'how long does it take').
Filter question keywords to a realistic difficulty band (the source used KD 0–40) to find terms a small site could target.
Check the intent label for each question. The source shows the intent field telling you whether a query is informational, navigational or transactional.
Discard questions irrelevant to your business context — the source excludes a celebrity/host query as off-topic and says to stick to general, relevant terms.
Sort the remaining list by search volume to prioritise, then shape content around the wording of the questions so those terms can rank and gain visibility.
For each chosen question, inspect which competitors hold the top positions and whether AI overviews, People Also Ask or authoritative blogs dominate the result before committing resource.
caveats: The source's specific volumes and difficulty values belong to its demo term, not your niche.
The presenter distinguishes informational, navigational and transactional queries as loose intent categories, not precise measurement.

cards.title: Assess competitor authority and SERP features before choosing a keyword
cards.summary: Check who already ranks and whether AI overviews or People Also Ask appear before deciding a keyword is worth pursuing.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a target product or content keyword is realistically winnable for your store.
steps: Search the candidate keyword and inspect the first-page results. The source's example for 'what is SEO' returned an AI overview, People Also Ask, and a well-known blog.

Identify the domains ranking. In the demonstration they included a high-authority SEO blog (domain authority 91/100), Wikipedia, Reddit, Mailchimp and others — the source notes such sites are not beaten in a day because they have age and qualified writers.
Apply intent filters in the keyword tool (e.g. transactional/commercial) to see whether buying-intent queries even exist for your topic before writing.
If high-authority and community platforms dominate the term, prefer lower-difficulty or less-crowded alternatives rather than fighting for a term where you appear nowhere in the top 100.
For each surviving keyword, note intent so the page you build matches the query type (definition, comparison, or purchase).
caveats: Domain authority and SERP layouts change constantly; the 91/100 figure is one moment in one niche.
Presence of an AI overview may reduce clicks, but the source does not quantify that effect; do not treat it as a hard rule that the keyword is unusable.

cards.title: Build a practice store on Blogger to learn SEO hands-on
cards.summary: Create a free Blogspot site to practise permalinks, internal links, menus and tracking installation before touching a live store.
cards.use_when: Learning or testing SEO mechanics (URL structure, internal linking, nofollow) without risk to your production ecommerce site.
steps: Create a blog in Blogger with a chosen name and address; the source shows how a name like 'SEO digital marketing news' becomes a blogspot.com URL.
Choose a theme and publish a test post. Avoid copying content verbatim — the presenter flags their own paste-through as a test only, not a practice to follow.

Use the post editor to set labels (acting as tags), a publish date, and a short, specific permalink. The source advises against using an entire long title in the URL and shows the 'custom permalink' option for editing it.

Practise internal linking: select anchor text, use the insert/edit link option, choose whether the link opens in a new window, and set follow/nofollow. The source states dofollow links are important for SEO because they pass a chance of ranking, nofollow does not, and the default is dofollow.
Create pages (not just posts) and add them to the site menu via the Layout section, toggling the page-list widget on so navigation appears.
Use the preview function before publishing to check layout, images and links.
Verify current Blogger menu names before relying on any specific path.
caveats: This is a sandbox exercise, not a recommendation to run a store on Blogspot.
The source notes Blogger pages have layout limitations (e.g. no permalink control on pages).

cards.title: Choose a content format matched to the query and buyer stage
cards.summary: Listicles, how-to guides, blogs, video, opinion pieces and infographics each serve different search intents and commercial purposes.
cards.use_when: Deciding what format to publish for a store's content calendar — category education, product guides or brand-building.
steps: Use listicles for scannable roundups (source example: '10 proven SEO techniques to boost your ranking in 2025') where readers want ranked options — useful for category or 'best of' style pages that support product browsing.

Use how-to guides for step-by-step tutorials, requiring clarity and concision, e.g. 'how to submit your website to Google Search Console step-by-step'. Good for setup, care or usage content around physical products.
Use blogs for engagement and trust-building with well-written, relevant discussion pieces; the source notes blogs establish authority, credibility and relationships.
Use video for demonstrations where showing beats telling, but the source insists video must be relevant and systematic — if it doesn't actually answer the query, viewers won't come.
Use opinion pieces to share unique perspectives and position the brand as a thought leader, encouraging discussion.
Use infographics to visualise data, stats or timelines — the source's examples chart algorithm changes or AI adoption year by year.
Match format to intent: transactional shoppers often need comparisons and guides, while informational searchers want definitions and how-tos.
caveats: The source gives no evidence about which format converts better for ecommerce; treat format choice as fit-to-query, not a proven sales lever.

cards.title: Apply personalization and localization to store content and offers
cards.summary: Personalization uses shopper details to prioritise relevance; localization targets the right message to the right region at the right time.
cards.use_when: Adapting PDP copy, offers or messaging for specific regions, languages or returning customers.
steps: For personalization, capture and use shopper details (first name, last name, address, phone, messages/concerns) as the source demonstrates at the add-to-cart stage, to make marketing prioritise the individual customer.

For localization, define it as sending the right message at the right time to the right customer, then build region-specific offers. The source's coaching example targets local students with a 20–30% discount for board-exam prep — translate that principle into region-specific ecommerce promotions where relevant.
Speak the language of international customers and provide multilingual chat support. The source shows sites where users pick English US/UK/Asia, then country, then state, before chat appears.
Use complete business listings as a localization tactic — full business details help local discovery.
Use AI assistance to personalise and localise content, since the source notes AI understands that there is intent behind a search (buying a washing machine, then searching how to use it).
Validate that the localized offer is legally and logistically serviceable in that region before publishing.
caveats: The discount percentages come from a coaching example; they are not benchmarks for ecommerce.
Personalisation depends on consent and lawful data handling, which the source does not address.

cards.title: Read engagement, bounce and conversion metrics by page in GA4
cards.summary: Use engagement rate, bounce rate and ecommerce purchase data at page level to find which store pages hold attention and drive purchases.
cards.use_when: Diagnosing which product, blog or landing pages hold shoppers and which lose them, as a basis for content and PDP improvements.
steps: Open the pages report rather than a channel report when you want to know which pages people spend time on — the source explains channel view won't show per-page time.
Sort by engagement rate. The source shows a blog page at 100% engagement with users sticking around, interpreted as useful content, and a correspondingly 0% bounce rate.

Cross-check ecommerce purchases under monetization. In the demonstration, 4,486 items had been purchased and one lotion SKU accounted for 96 items, shown as 2.14% of the total — the source cautions this is not the correct conversion rate.

Get the real transaction conversion rate from a data-studio style report or filtered view, because the default ecommerce table percentage is not the same as transaction conversion. In the source's data studio example the overall conversion rate was shown as 26.8K with a 43% improvement over the comparison period, and a user conversion rate of 99.9% — treat these as report-specific outputs.
For click-through rate, use Google Search Console; for traffic channels and frequency, use GA acquisition reports.
Export the page-level data (the source uses export to Google Sheets) and compute period-over-period differences to find pages with declining traffic to focus on.
caveats: The source's numbers belong to one skincare website and are not benchmarks.
GA4 and data studio interfaces change; verify current report paths and metric definitions before trusting a figure.
Distinguish engagement rate, bounce rate and transaction conversion rate — the source explicitly warns the default ecommerce-table percentage is not the true conversion rate.

cards.title: Spot declining pages by comparing active users period over period
cards.summary: Export page-level traffic for two periods and subtract to surface pages losing users so you can prioritise their recovery.
cards.use_when: Monthly ecommerce content and SEO review to find PDPs, category pages or blog posts that are losing organic traffic.
steps: In GA4, open acquisition traffic and select your reporting month, comparing with the previous period.
Remove the channel breakdown and add page/screen as the dimension so each row is a page.
Export to Google Sheets. Set current-period and previous-period columns side by side.
Compute the difference (current minus previous) in a new column — pressing equals and clicking the cells auto-fills the reference.
Select the difference column and sort Z to A to see the pages with the biggest drop first. The source describes these as the important pages to focus on next month to recover traffic.
Ignore noise pages like account/login, which the source says people don't target for SEO and which shouldn't distract from commercial pages.
Repeat the process monthly and keep the sheet as a rolling log.
caveats: The source's example comparison windows are arbitrary (e.g. 1 October vs previous 31 days); choose windows that match your seasonality.
A difference column alone doesn't explain cause — pair it with Search Console before acting.

cards.title: Install GA4 by adding the measurement tag to the site head
cards.summary: Create a GA4 property, place the Google tag in the head, then verify installation in real time.
cards.use_when: Setting up analytics on a new or redesigned storefront so you can see traffic, behaviour and ecommerce revenue.
steps: Sign in to Google Analytics with a Google ID and open Admin (bottom-left gear). Under the account column choose create, name the account, click next.

Enter property details: property name, reporting time zone and currency. The source notes the currency matters for ecommerce and advises setting it up properly now even if you won't use it immediately.

Choose business details and business objectives. The source notes you cannot leave other objectives checked when selecting one — it recommends selecting the relevant ones such as generate leads, drive sales, understand traffic, and engagement/retention.
Accept the terms, select the Web platform, and enter the website URL and stream name to create the data stream.

From the data stream, view tag instructions and choose manual installation to reveal the Google tag snippet. In a Blogger back end the source pastes it under the theme's HTML head section; on other platforms place it immediately after the opening head tag.
The source warns: do not add more than one Google tag per page.

Verify installation: click the test button in the setup flow, then open Reports > Realtime overview and confirm views appear — the source also checks page source (Ctrl+U, then find) to confirm the tag is present.
caveats: Google Analytics and CMS interfaces change frequently; verify the current setup flow and tag format.
Realtime test results are momentary; the source shows 'views 1' from the presenter's own visit, which confirms installation but not production traffic.

cards.title: Size the SEO opportunity with GA4 channel comparison
cards.summary: Compare organic channel users and sessions across two periods to see whether SEO is growing or slipping.
cards.use_when: Reporting store SEO performance to stakeholders or deciding whether to invest more in organic content.
steps: In the property that has traffic, open Reports > Acquisition > Traffic acquisition and set the date range (the source used one month) with compare to previous period toggled on.

Remove page-level rows so channels are visible, then look at the Organic channel. The source's example showed active users at 8,000 versus 5,000 previously, a 59% improvement, with sessions of roughly 9,000 versus 6,000.
Drill into organic pages to see where the traffic came from, then export to Google Sheets for further comparison of active users by page across periods.
Compare current and previous columns to identify whether organic growth is broad or concentrated in a few pages.
Confirm the data stream is actively collecting (the source shows 'data actively collecting past 48 hours' as a health check).
caveats: The source's channel figures are one account's example, not a benchmark.
Organic session counts do not equal revenue; combine with monetization data before judging SEO ROI.

cards.title: Create and verify a Google Business Profile for local store discovery
cards.summary: A verified Google Business Profile places your store in maps and local packs, which matters for local and mobile searchers.
cards.use_when: Setting up or improving local SEO so nearby shoppers can find your store or service area.
steps: Start a Google Business Profile, name the business and pick a category that matches how customers search (the source uses a marketing agency example).

Decide whether customers can visit a location. If yes, add the address: street, city, postcode and state. If you're an online-only business, the source demonstrates selecting no for location and no for delivery/visits.
Place and confirm the map pin, add a phone number, and choose whether to verify now or later. The source emphasises that a profile only becomes visible after verification.
Add services or products the store offers (the source lists affiliate marketing, branding, SEO, digital marketing as examples) and set opening hours.
Write a business description and upload images. The source fills these to complete the profile.
Once verified, the listing appears in local packs, Google Maps and mobile search, and supports voice assistant results — the source's client example shows name, address and phone displayed.
caveats: Verification requirements and available fields change; verify the current Google Business Profile flow.
The source's example business address is random and not a real listing.

cards.title: Use Google Search Console for crawl issues and indexing health
cards.summary: Search Console complements analytics by surfacing crawl errors, 404s and indexing status that GA4 does not show.
cards.use_when: Investigating why store pages are not being indexed or why organic impressions diverge from your expectations.
steps: Sign in to Google Search Console with the same Google ID used for analytics, then review the overview page.
Read the performance graph for queries and clicks, and the indexing report for how many pages are indexed versus not indexed. The source describes these as the two core views.
Install the verification code (the source demonstrates the account setup and code installation step-by-step).
Submit the XML sitemap within Search Console so crawlers can discover store URLs faster.
Check for 404 pages and other crawl errors, which the source identifies as a primary Search Console use case.
Use Search Console, not GA4, for click-through rate analysis at query level.
caveats: Search Console data is sampled and delayed, and the interface changes; verify current report names.
Search Console shows impressions and clicks, not revenue or add-to-cart behaviour — combine with GA4.

cards.title: Treat CTR, dwell time and conversion as the behavioural signals Google weighs
cards.summary: Click-through rate, time on page and conversion rate are the user-behaviour signals the source highlights for SEO and commercial performance.
cards.use_when: Judging whether a store page is performing and deciding what to improve on a landing page or PDP.
steps: Track click-through rate in Google Search Console. The source's opinion is that a longer (higher) click-through rate correlates with more conversions — treat this as the presenter's claim, not a proven formula.
Track duration on page. The source suggests staying roughly 2–5 minutes signals something useful is there, but presents this as an informal rule of thumb rather than a benchmark.
Track conversion rate and check it in Analytics, using a data-studio style report for the genuine transaction conversion rate rather than the default ecommerce table figure.
Check frequency of visits and navigation channel (organic versus other mediums) to understand how shoppers arrive.

If you're saturated with competition, the source's advice is to improve existing products/services, offer meaningful discounts (e.g. 20–30%) and revisit pricing models rather than assume SEO alone will rescue you.
caveats: The 2–5 minute dwell target is the source's heuristic, not an established benchmark.
The link between CTR and conversion is stated as an opinion; it should be tested rather than assumed.

cards.title: Plan visually with mapping tools, but build strategy from competitor analysis
cards.summary: Visual site-mapping tools help structure a store's pages and keywords, but the source insists strategy comes from human analysis of competitors, not tool output alone.
cards.use_when: Planning a store's information architecture, category tree or keyword map before a build or migration.
steps: Use a visual sitemap builder (e.g. WriteMaps) to plan website pages and gather content into a sitemap without drawing every node by hand.

Consider collaborative mapping tools (the source names MindNode) for keyword research and tracking data as inputs to SEO strategy; other tools mentioned include streamingfrog, Slickplan, Dynomapper and RankMath.
Treat tool output as insight only. The source states no tool can create a strategy directly — the strategy is the manual work of analysing human behaviour and competitor activity.
For a large store, rely on CMS automation to cover the structure and navigation rather than mapping thousands of product pages manually.
Cross-check any planned architecture against how your CMS actually generates URLs (Shopify products/collections vs WordPress posts/pages).
caveats: Tool names and features will age; verify current offerings before adopting.
The source does not claim these tools cause ranking improvements — they are planning aids.

cards.title: Prioritise low-difficulty, high-volume terms over vanity head keywords
cards.summary: The source's core keyword principle: pick terms with good volume and low difficulty so a store can gain visibility rather than chasing unwinnable head terms.
cards.use_when: Deciding which terms to target for a new store or a new category where you currently have no ranking.
steps: Start by sorting candidate keywords by volume in descending order to see the biggest opportunities.
Then apply the difficulty lens. The source warns that directly targeting a very high-competition keyword is very difficult — you may not appear anywhere in the top 100 pages.

For a first phase, filter to lower difficulty terms (the source uses 0–40 KD) and choose those with decent volume. The source's own phrasing is: choose keywords with good volume and low difficulty so it's easier to get visibility.
Reject terms that don't match your service footprint — don't target local terms for cities you don't serve.
Check the intent label for each shortlisted term and make sure the content or page type you'll build matches it.
Re-rank your shortlist by the balance of volume and difficulty rather than volume alone, and revisit the list as your authority grows.
caveats: KD bands are tool-specific; 0–40 is the source's demonstration range, not a universal rule.
The source gives no numeric volume thresholds, so judge volume relative to your market.

cards.title: Reference the sitemap in robots.txt to control crawling and discovery
cards.summary: robots.txt hides unwanted pages from crawlers and can also point crawlers to your sitemap, combining exclusion and discovery in one file.
cards.use_when: Configuring a store's robots.txt after launch or a site migration so Google crawls product pages but skips non-indexable URLs.
steps: Open the store's robots.txt and check whether the sitemap URL is included. The source finds an example where the sitemap reference is present and explains it lets anyone find the sitemap from that file.
Use robots.txt directives to hide pages you don't want Google to crawl (the source describes this as the file's exclusion purpose).
Keep the sitemap reference as a standard syntax so Google can fetch the sitemap automatically via the file.
Do not block product, category or other indexable pages with robots.txt — exclusion is for pages that should not appear in search at all.
Confirm the final file in a browser and in Search Console's robots report, since the source notes free tools previously took far more time for what is now a single file.
Re-verify the syntax and the sitemap path after any CMS or domain change.
caveats: robots.txt directives differ in effect (disallow vs noindex); blocking crawling is not the same as removing pages from the index.
Sitemap paths are CMS-specific (e.g. sitemap_index.xml), so verify your exact URL.

cards.title: Treat canonical URLs as the single version of each store page
cards.summary: Canonical URLs identify the single preferred version of a page's content, preventing duplicate versions from splitting ranking signals.
cards.use_when: Reviewing a store with filter, pagination or parameter variants that create near-duplicate product URLs.
steps: Understand the source's definition: canonical URLs are the URLs that show a unique page or unique content — the version a page intends to be indexed under.
Check a live page's source code for the canonical tag. The source shows a page whose canonical version points to itself, meaning it isn't treated as duplicated elsewhere.
Expect the XML sitemap to list these canonical versions of your pages, so the sitemap and canonical tags reinforce the same preferred URLs.
Where a store generates variant URLs (filters, tracking parameters, sort orders), plan to consolidate them to the canonical product or category URL.
Verify the implementation after changing it, since incorrect canonical tags can deindex the wrong page.
caveats: The source covers canonicals only briefly; it does not prescribe implementation for complex ecommerce parameter setups.
Canonical tags are hints, not guarantees, and should be paired with consistent internal linking.

cards.title: Understand where SEO tracking tools fit before wiring them up
cards.summary: GA4, Search Console and Tag Manager are the three core tracking pillars the source recommends for SEO measurement, feeding audits, meta tags and event tracking.
cards.use_when: Planning the tracking stack for a new store or auditing gaps before running SEO and conversion experiments.
steps: Install Google Analytics 4 for traffic and user behaviour.
Install Google Search Console for crawl issues, indexing and query-level performance.
Install Google Tag Manager so you can deploy tags (including rich snippet code and meta tags) without editing site code on every change.
Plan to use Tag Manager to deploy schema/rich snippet code on the store without touching the theme, and to set up ecommerce event tracking such as add-to-cart button tracking.
Run technical and on-page audits (the source uses Ahrefs for its site audit) to identify gaps in on-page and technical SEO.
Use a backlink audit tool and a keyword tool (the source mentions SEMrush) alongside the tracking stack, and build the tracking code into pages at launch rather than retrofitting later.
caveats: This card describes the source's agenda for the session; the specific Tag Manager and rich-snippet processes are covered elsewhere in the course.
Tool capabilities change; verify current Tag Manager tag templates and GA4 event names.

cards.title: Prepare store content for AI-assisted and voice search
cards.summary: Search is shifting toward AI overviews, People Also Ask and voice, which changes how content should be written and how page speed is assessed.
cards.use_when: Planning content and page experience for a store that wants visibility in AI overviews and voice assistant results.
steps: Write to intent. The source repeats that intent is very important and that AI understands queries such as buying a washing machine and then asking how to use it — so cover both purchase and post-purchase questions.

Structure content so it can be pulled into AI overviews and People Also Ask, using clear question headings and direct answers (the source demonstrates distinguishing informational, transactional and commercial queries).
Optimise page experience for both desktop and mobile separately, because Google reports two page-speed scores — the source attributes this to the shift to smartphone search.
Recognise that AI collects and analyses user behaviour data to improve ranking, so behavioural signals matter alongside content quality.
Voice results depend on a recognisable brand name and relevant terms, so keep brand and offering language consistent across pages and listings.
Verify current AI overview and voice result formats, as they change frequently.
caveats: The source does not provide measured effects of AI overviews on ecommerce clicks; the advice is directional.
AI and voice search behaviour is evolving quickly, so revisit these tactics regularly.

cards.title: Edit permalinks to keep product and post URLs short and specific
cards.summary: Long title-based URLs are discouraged; custom permalinks let you shorten and specify the URL for a page.
cards.use_when: Publishing a new product, category or blog page where the default URL would be a long version of the title.
steps: When publishing, inspect the auto-generated permalink. The source shows Blogger taking the full title as the URL by default.
If the title is long, open the custom permalink option and replace it with a short, specific slug (the source uses 'brand perception').
Keep the slug meaningful and aligned to the page's topic rather than a full sentence or keyword-stuffed string.
Confirm the final URL before publishing, since changing it after indexing can create broken links or duplicate URLs.
Note the CMS limitation: the source finds Blogger pages do not offer the same URL structure controls as posts, so check your platform's options.
After publishing, verify the live URL and update any internal links that point to the old path.
caveats: Changing permalinks on already-indexed store URLs requires redirects, which the source does not cover.
Blogger-specific limitations are described; other platforms (Shopify, WordPress) have different permalink controls.

cards.title: Set follow/nofollow deliberately when building internal links
cards.summary: Dofollow links pass ranking opportunity while nofollow links do not; the default is dofollow and should be reserved for pages you want to strengthen.
cards.use_when: Adding internal links between product pages, categories and blog content, or managing outbound links on a store.
steps: When inserting a link in your CMS editor, locate the insert/edit link option, paste the target URL, and choose whether it opens in a new window. The source notes opening in the same window loses the previous page.

Set the rel attribute intentionally: the source states dofollow links are important in SEO because they give a chance of ranking, while nofollow links do not follow SEO guidelines. Every link is dofollow by default.
Keep internal links between your own commercial pages as dofollow so ranking signals flow to product and category pages you care about.
Consider nofollow for untrusted outbound links or links you do not want to endorse.
Follow the source's principle that links should be helpful internal links — link where the target genuinely helps the reader, not everywhere.
Recheck rel attributes after CMS or theme updates, since editors sometimes reset defaults.
caveats: The source describes dofollow/nofollow in simple terms; modern search engines treat nofollow as a hint rather than an absolute rule.
The benefit of dofollow links is stated as the presenter's explanation, without measured evidence.
